findings.title: Repository read access grants administrative and mutation authority
findings.description: The authorization middleware uses the same identity.CanAccess(repositoryId) predicate for all repository operations, regardless of HTTP method or effect. Consequently, an identity permitted to view a repository is also permitted to update or archive its registration and to invoke the numerous metadata, review-job, and third-party mutations mapped below. Only repository creation/import receives a separate CanRegisterRepositories check, demonstrating that no corresponding write or administrative permission is required for existing repositories.
findings.recommendation: Define explicit operation-level policies such as repository read, metadata write, review execution, handover, and repository administration. Enforce the appropriate policy on each endpoint, and reserve registration updates and archival for identities with repository-administration authority.

findings.title: Authenticated callers can forge reviewer attribution
findings.description: Finding-state changes persist request.Author as the actor, and thread entries persist request.HumanName as a human author. Neither value is bound to the authenticated identity established by ApiSecurity. Any caller with repository access can therefore impersonate another reviewer in durable review metadata and audit logs.
findings.recommendation: Derive the authoritative actor identifier and display name from ApiSecurity.Identity(context). If a caller-supplied display label is needed, store it separately as untrusted presentation data and retain the authenticated subject identifier for audit purposes.

findings.title: File endpoint buffers repository files without a size limit
findings.description: FileContent calls File.ReadAllBytesAsync on the selected file and then decodes the complete byte array into a string. The configured request-body limit does not constrain response-side file reads. A sufficiently large file in an accessible repository can therefore cause large simultaneous byte-array and string allocations, allowing an authenticated caller to exhaust process memory through repeated requests.
findings.recommendation: Check file length against a configured response/read limit before allocation, reject oversized files with 413 or 422, and consider bounded streaming or paginated line retrieval. Apply a per-client request-rate policy to this resource-intensive endpoint as defense in depth.

findings.title: Dangling symbolic links bypass reparse-point rejection
findings.description: A component is inspected for FileAttributes.ReparsePoint only when Directory.Exists or File.Exists returns true. Both existence checks can return false for a dangling symbolic link, causing that component to be skipped. If its external target subsequently exists, or is created before the validated candidate is used, access through the candidate can leave the configured root despite successful validation.
findings.recommendation: Inspect every path component using link-aware metadata that does not follow the link and can identify dangling symbolic links or Windows reparse points. For operations that create missing paths, reject unresolved intermediate components unless their ancestry has been securely established.

findings.title: Reparse-point validation is vulnerable to a check-to-use race
findings.description: The method checks path components by name and then returns without retaining filesystem handles or performing the protected operation. An attacker able to modify an inspected directory can replace it with a symbolic link or junction after its attributes are checked but before the caller opens the candidate, redirecting the eventual operation outside the root.
findings.recommendation: Combine traversal and the protected filesystem operation using securely opened directory handles and no-follow/beneath-root semantics appropriate to the platform. If that is not possible, keep every ancestor pinned by handle, verify identities after opening, and operate relative to those handles rather than treating this method as an authorization boundary.

findings.title: Repository symlinks can trigger out-of-root and unbounded file reads
findings.description: Enumerated repository paths are combined lexically with the repository root and then opened without resolving symbolic links or verifying that the resolved target remains inside the repository. Git repositories can contain symbolic links, and File.Exists does not enforce containment. An attacker controlling repository contents can therefore make a text-extension path reference a host file outside the repository. The service reads that target and derives its size, line count, and normalized SHA-256 fingerprint; two links to the same target can cause the fingerprint to appear as a duplication candidate. A link to a zero-length-reported stream such as a device or procfs entry can also bypass the 4 MiB metadata check and make ReadAllText consume unbounded data, enabling denial of service.
findings.recommendation: Reject symbolic links and reparse points during enumeration, or resolve each target and verify its canonical path is contained beneath the canonical repository root immediately before opening it. Open files through a bounded stream and stop after the permitted byte limit instead of relying on FileInfo.Length. Apply the same resolved-target validation to coverage reports and project files.

findings.title: Repository-derived module names are injected into AI instructions
findings.description: ArchitectureReviewContext interpolates module names from the repository hierarchy directly into an instruction-bearing prompt. A repository-controlled module name can contain instruction-like text or control characters, causing the downstream model to treat data as directives and potentially suppress, fabricate, or redirect review findings. The surrounding statement that the edges are deterministic does not establish a machine-enforced data boundary.
findings.recommendation: Serialize dependency edges as structured data with strict field and length validation, remove or escape control characters, and place them in a clearly delimited untrusted-data section. The higher-priority model instruction should explicitly require treating every edge field as data and ignoring directives contained within it.

findings.title: Reparse-point confinement can be bypassed through a check-to-use race
findings.description: NormalizeRelativePath checks the current path with RejectReparseTraversal and returns a relative string. ResolveFile then reconstructs and checks that pathname, ultimately returning it for still-later use; metadata methods likewise pass the pathname to another component after validation. A party able to modify repository entries concurrently can replace a checked file or directory with a symbolic link or junction between validation and access, causing the subsequent operation to traverse outside the configured repository root. The explicit reparse-point rejection demonstrates that untrusted links are in scope, but the pathname-based check does not preserve that guarantee through use.
findings.recommendation: Perform validation and access as one safe operation using directory/file handles and no-follow semantics, walking each component relative to an already-open repository-root handle. Return or consume the opened handle rather than a re-resolvable pathname. Where the platform cannot provide an atomic primitive, isolate repositories from concurrent untrusted mutation and revalidate the opened object's resolved identity before reading it.

findings.title: Repository requests can supply executable sensor commands

Any sensor runner that honors the stored command will execute authority supplied by the request rather than by trusted server configuration.

Do not accept command lines, executable paths, arguments, report paths, or working directories directly from repository-registration requests; construct them from trusted server-side definitions. findings.title: Validated repository paths can be replaced before use

findings.title: Unbounded sidecar parsing permits resource exhaustion
findings.description: Every matching repository file is loaded completely into a string and then parsed into a JSON DOM without any file-size, nesting-depth, or aggregate-index limit. A repository containing one very large sidecar, or many large sidecars, can force excessive allocation and parsing work synchronously during index construction and again on filesystem events, potentially exhausting memory or making the service unavailable.
findings.recommendation: Reject sidecars above a conservative byte limit before reading them, configure an appropriate JSON maximum depth, and cap aggregate indexed payload size or document count. Prefer bounded streaming or byte-based parsing so the file is not simultaneously retained as both a string and a JSON DOM.

findings.title: Invalid file updates leave previously trusted metadata indexed
findings.description: When an already indexed sidecar is replaced with malformed JSON or loses required fields, Update exits or catches the parsing error without removing the existing dictionary entry. The old payload can therefore continue to be returned by Read indefinitely, while Find may return the path of the now-invalid replacement. This allows stale review evidence to remain authoritative after its backing data has been revoked or changed.
findings.recommendation: Invalidate the existing entry when a definitive update cannot be validated. To tolerate transient atomic-write states, debounce and retry updates for a bounded period, then remove the old entry if the file remains invalid or unreadable.

findings.title: Filesystem links can redirect archive access outside the repository
findings.description: The archive root and run directories are constructed lexically and then passed directly to filesystem APIs. No component is resolved and checked for containment, and symbolic links, junctions, or other reparse points are not rejected. An attacker able to control repository filesystem contents can place a link at the archive root, month, run, or archive-file level and cause create, append, or read operations to follow it outside the intended `.quality/run-history` boundary. Create-only mode prevents replacement of an existing destination file but does not prevent creation in a redirected directory; append and read operations also follow redirected paths.
findings.recommendation: Resolve and validate the real filesystem target beneath a trusted canonical archive root before every operation, reject symbolic links and reparse points in all path components, and use no-follow or handle-relative filesystem operations where supported. Consider storing security-sensitive archive data outside repository-controlled paths.

findings.title: Unbounded archive loading permits resource-exhaustion denial of service

A repository contributor or compromised process can create oversized or numerous archive records that consume excessive memory and CPU whenever these public loading methods are invoked.
findings.recommendation: Set explicit maximum file sizes, JSON-line lengths, record counts, and aggregate bytes before deserialization. Stream records where possible, reject oversized files before reading them, and apply cancellation or processing budgets to archive enumeration.

findings.recommendation: Enforce conservative maximum sizes before reading run artifacts, deserialize from a bounded stream, cap collection and string lengths where practical, and reject oversized files with a controlled load failure.

Agent judgement: The boundary sensor blocks the unit due to numerous request-to-filesystem flows and an unauthenticated health boundary. Independent review also found a repository-scope authorization bypass, disclosure of host-wide quota information, unencrypted downstream transport support, unbounded file loading, and insufficient throttling of expensive scans. Secret scanning passed, but dependency and ESLint analysis were unavailable, and test coverage is unknown.

observations.summary: At least one required machine sensor was unavailable; this review is not a clean result. The security posture is blocking. Existing path-confinement, constant-time credential comparison, request-size limits, exception sanitization, repository filtering, and rate limiting provide useful defenses, but they do not offset the sensor-reported boundary failures or the additional authorization and resource-exhaustion defects. Most importantly, a repository-scoped client can repoint an authorized repository ID to another allowed root, defeating repository isolation. Dependency assurance remains incomplete because the dependency sensor was unavailable.

findings.title: Repository-scoped clients can repoint an authorized repository ID
findings.description: The middleware requires CanRegisterRepositories only when creating a repository or importing from Agent Studio. PUT /api/repos/{repoId} instead requires only access to the existing repoId, then passes an attacker-controlled RootPath to UpdateAsync. Consequently, a client scoped to one repository can change that registration to any other configured allowed root and subsequently access the new root through the still-authorized ID. This defeats repository-level isolation. The same authorization gap also permits repository-scoped clients to archive registrations.
findings.recommendation: Require a distinct repository-administration capability, such as CanRegisterRepositories, for updating or archiving registrations. When changing RootPath or GlobalInputsDirectory, additionally authorize the caller for the destination or prohibit those fields from repository-scoped updates.

findings.title: Any authenticated client can read host-wide provider quota data
findings.description: The authorization middleware explicitly exempts /api/quotas from repository-access checks. The endpoint exposes global Claude OAuth and Codex session quota details, including plan, usage, limits, errors, sources, and reset times. A client authorized for an unrelated repository can therefore inspect host-wide account and operational information.
findings.recommendation: Protect quota data with an explicit host-operator capability. If repository clients need quota information, return only a repository-scoped or minimally aggregated view that does not expose provider account details.

findings.title: Agent Studio integration permits unencrypted HTTP destinations
findings.description: Target validation accepts every absolute URI rather than requiring HTTPS. CreateTaskAsync then transmits finding summaries, finding text, repository paths, metadata references, project identity, and the configured client identifier to that URI. An http:// configuration exposes this material to interception or modification in transit.
findings.recommendation: Require an https URI for non-loopback Agent Studio targets. If cleartext loopback communication is required for local development, encode that as a narrow explicit exception and reject other schemes and hosts.

findings.title: File endpoint loads and serializes repository files without a size limit
findings.description: FileContent reads the complete selected file into a byte array, decodes it into a second full-size string, and returns it through JSON without checking its size. The configured MaxRequestBodyBytes limits inbound bodies only. An authenticated caller can repeatedly select a very large repository file and cause substantial memory allocation and response amplification.
findings.recommendation: Enforce a conservative maximum readable file size before allocating content, return 413 or 422 when exceeded, and consider bounded streaming for supported file types. Apply a response-size and per-client throughput policy to the endpoint.

findings.title: Expensive scan endpoints lack the spend rate-limit policy
findings.description: Repository scans, secret scans, and arbitrary enabled sensor scans can recursively inspect repositories or launch external tools, but their routes do not apply the spend policy used by reviews and handovers. The global limiter only caps concurrent requests and has no replenishment window, so an authenticated client can continuously occupy available slots and repeatedly launch expensive work.
findings.recommendation: Apply a per-identity fixed-window or token-bucket policy to all scan endpoints, including GET endpoints that initiate computation. Limit concurrent scans per repository and coalesce or reject duplicate in-flight scans.

findings.title: Request-bound value reaches a filesystem or process surface
findings.description: GET /api/security/attack-coverage combines request input with filesystem-read.
findings.recommendation: Keep path/process arguments on a confined allowlisted data flow and verify the confinement before the sink.

findings.title: Inbound boundary has no derived authorization
findings.description: GET /health is externally callable, but the inventory could not derive an authentication and authorization requirement.
findings.recommendation: Apply an explicit authentication and authorization policy, or document and mechanically encode the narrow public exception.
